nameStory: The white-faced meadowhawk gets its memorable name from the males' striking snow-white face, which stands out like a bright beacon against their red bodies. The "meadowhawk" part reflects their hunting behavior - these dragonflies patrol open meadows and fields like aerial hawks, swooping down to snatch up flying insects.
description: The white-faced meadowhawk is a medium-sized dragonfly that's one of our most distinctive late-season fliers. Adult males are eye-catching with their brilliant red bodies contrasted by pure white faces that almost seem to glow in sunlight. Females look quite different, sporting yellowish or brown bodies that help them blend in while laying eggs. These dragonflies are part of the skimmer family, known for their habit of perching frequently on vegetation while hunting.

idTips.label: Male's White Face
idTips.description: Adult males have a strikingly pure white face that looks almost chalky or painted on - much brighter white than any other dragonfly you'll see in New England

idTips.label: Male's Red Body
idTips.description: Mature males develop bright red abdomens and thorax that feel smooth and slightly waxy when gently touched, creating a vivid contrast with the white face

idTips.label: Female Coloration
idTips.description: Females are yellowish-brown to tan colored overall, lacking the dramatic red and white pattern of males but sharing the same body shape and size

idTips.label: Wing Position at Rest
idTips.description: When perched, wings are held horizontally out from the body like other skimmers, rather than folded back along the abdomen

idTips.label: Body Texture
idTips.description: The abdomen feels firm and slightly cylindrical when gently handled, with a smooth surface that has a subtle waxy feel

habitat: White-faced meadowhawks prefer open areas near water sources like ponds, marshes, slow streams, and boggy areas throughout New England. You'll often spot them perching on tall grasses, shrubs, or fence posts in meadows and fields adjacent to wetlands. They favor areas with a mix of open water for breeding and nearby grasslands or clearings for hunting.

seasonality.spring: Not typically seen in spring as adults emerge later in the season. Any meadowhawks spotted in early spring are likely overwintered individuals of other species.
seasonality.summer: Adults begin emerging in mid to late summer, with males developing their distinctive white faces and red coloration as they mature. Peak activity occurs in August.
seasonality.fall: This is prime white-faced meadowhawk season, with fully mature adults at their most colorful and active from September into October. They're often one of the last dragonflies flying before frost.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts. Eggs overwinter in mud or vegetation near water, waiting for spring warmth to begin development.

funFact: Male white-faced meadowhawks can actually change the intensity of their face color - the white becomes more brilliant and almost seems to glow when they're actively defending territory or courting females, like having a built-in mood ring on their face!
confusionNotes: The bright white face of males makes them nearly unmistakable, but females can be confused with other brown meadowhawks. Remember the simple rule: if it has a white face and red body, it's definitely a white-faced meadowhawk male - no other dragonfly in New England has this combination.
compareHints: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, the white-faced is the only one where males develop a pure white face - other meadowhawks have reddish, yellowish, or dark faces. The ruby meadowhawk male also turns red but keeps a reddish face, while autumn meadowhawks have distinctive yellow-orange faces that never turn white.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the seven meadowhawk species in New England, Autumn Meadowhawks are distinguished by their completely yellow legs - most other meadowhawks have black legs or black stripes on their legs.

Among New England meadowhawks, the band-winged is the only one with prominent dark wing bands - ruby meadowhawks have clear wings and bright red males, while autumn meadowhawks lack wing bands and have more orange-red coloring.

Among New England's meadowhawks, the Saffron-winged is most easily distinguished by its golden wing stripes in younger individuals and females, while the Ruby Meadowhawk typically shows clearer wings and the White-faced has a distinctly pale face.

Cherry-faced meadowhawks are distinguished from other meadowhawks primarily by their very dark red, almost burgundy faces when mature, compared to the brighter reds of ruby meadowhawks or the white faces of white-faced meadowhawks.
